title: Switzerland Without Us
summary: This view takes away the human changes collected on this site. The first step shows the land about 1800, before industry. The second step shows the land before farming began, about 7,500 years ago. The map shows only changes that are in this collection, so the picture is not complete.

stops.title: Switzerland today: what people changed
text: Around 1700, wetlands and moors covered about 5 percent of the country. In the 19th and early 20th century, fens and raised bogs decreased by about 90 percent. Today they cover only about 0.5 percent of the land. Between 1885 and 1940, about 80,000 ha of moorland were drained. About 80,000 ha more followed during the Second World War.

About 90 percent of the floodplains (land beside rivers that floods often) disappeared since 1850. River works and intensive land use caused this. Almost all Swiss rivers were corrected in the 19th and early 20th century. The larger corrections in the HLS table alone add up to about 510 km of river (our own sum).

Today about one quarter of all river stretches are artificial, heavily changed or piped underground. On the Plateau (Mittelland), almost half of the rivers and streams are far from their natural state. In 2005, more than 100,000 barriers higher than 50 cm blocked fish and other animals.

Forest area decreased in the first half of the 19th century. After the federal forest law of 1876, the forest grew again. In the 20th century it increased by more than 40 percent. Today forest covers about 29.5 percent of the country, settlements about 8 percent. About 5 percent is sealed (covered by buildings, roads or other hard surfaces). In 1844 Switzerland had no railway; in 1995 the network was about 5,000 km long.

stops.title: About 1800: before industry
text: This step removes only the changes made after 1800. Older works stay on the map. One example is the Kander, which people led into Lake Thun in 1711-1714. Around 1800 there was no railway in Switzerland. The first line, from Zurich, ended at Baden in 1847. The background map is from 1864, so it already shows some later works, for example the Linth canal.

Many rivers in the wide valleys had several side arms. The later corrections closed these arms and gave each river one bed. The engineer Tulla wrote this rule in 1812. The Linth, for example, flowed in a winding and often changing bed through the Linth plain. In the 18th and 19th century, floods became more frequent, mainly because of a change in climate.

Large fens (wet meadows on peat, fed by groundwater) lay in the Bernese Seeland, the St. Gallen Rhine valley and many other river plains. The Grosses Moos covered about 100 km2. It was the largest continuous moor area in Switzerland. Weesen and Walenstadt flooded regularly, and the Linth plain became a marsh. Malaria (a fever disease) threatened the villages at the edge of the Linth plain and in the Seeland.

The lakes had their natural levels. The three Jura lakes were 2.5 m higher than after the first Jura water correction. St. Peter's Island in Lake Biel was still a real island. Lake Wauwil still existed; it was drained in the mid-19th century. Wood was almost the only fuel, and the forest area was getting smaller. Wolves, lynx and bears still lived in parts of the country. But bears and lynx had already left the Plateau. The last beaver was killed in the early 19th century.

stops.title: Before farming: about 7,500 years ago
text: This step removes every change in the collection, also the old ones. It shows the land before the first farmers. The Neolithic (the first farming period) began here about 5500 BC. Domestic sheep, goats, cattle and pigs appear from about 5400 BC. But cereal pollen exists from about 6500 BC. So the start of farming was slow, and the date is rounded.

Dense, closed forest covered most of the land. Open places were rare: moors, river gravel plains and places where storms had thrown down trees. In the lowlands grew mixed broadleaf forest with hazel, elm, oak, lime, ash and alder. Silver fir and beech spread after about 5500 BC. Later the Plateau got a mixed forest similar to today's.

In the Central Alps the forest grew higher than today. From about 9000 to 2500 BC, the timberline (upper edge of closed forest) lay 100-150 m above today's tree limit. At its highest, it reached about 2420 m. Later, alpine pastures lowered the upper forest limit. Natural wildfires are very rare north of the Alps. Lake mud shows that fires on the Plateau became more frequent with Neolithic farming.

The last hunters mostly hunted red deer, elk, roe deer, wild boar, aurochs (wild cattle), brown bear, wolf, fox, pine marten and wildcat. The wild horse had become rare. Wisent (European bison) and aurochs still lived on the Plateau in the Neolithic. Beavers lived in the plains, for example in the Rhone plain. Beavers build dams and so make new wetlands. Lake levels also changed naturally, possibly because of climate.
